sourceCourseTitle: Llmops Ai Observability Engineer / Quality Monitoring

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) Distinguish offline and online evaluation and when to use each 2) Design reliable offline test sets, rubrics, and metrics for LLMs 3) Plan safe, statistically sound online experiments with guardrails and monitoring

blocks.title: Continuously monitor your LLM apps in production
blocks.label: Course Video

body.en:
Offline evaluation uses static datasets, labeled rubrics, and automated metrics to compare prompts/models safely before deployment. Typical metrics include task accuracy/EM, F1 for extraction, ROUGE/BLEU/BERTScore for summarization, toxicity and bias scores for safety, hallucination/factuality checks (e.g., retrieval-grounded correctness), as well as latency and cost. Techniques include golden sets, pairwise preference judgments, Elo/Bradley–Terry ranking, stratified data slicing, bootstrap confidence intervals, and cross-validation. Control leakage by keeping train/eval splits clean, deduplicating near-duplicates, and mirroring real traffic distribution.

Online evaluation measures impact on real users and systems. Use canary or A/B tests (or bandits) with clear primary KPIs (e.g., task success, deflection rate, CSAT), guardrail metrics (safety incidents, latency SLOs, error rate), and budgets (cost per 1k tokens). Ensure randomization, eligibility rules, and exposure controls. Apply power analysis for sample size, sequential testing to detect early wins or stop for harm, and segment results by slices (locale, task type) to catch regressions. Monitor drift and feedback loops; combine explicit ratings with implicit signals (click-through, resolution, rephrases). Connect offline and online by using offline gates to shortlist candidates, then validate causal impact online and update offline suites based on online learnings.

• Offline evaluation: fixed datasets, human rubrics, and automated metrics to de-risk changes before deployment
• Online evaluation: randomized experiments on real traffic to measure KPIs, safety, latency, and cost
• Slicing and significance: analyze by critical cohorts and use confidence intervals/p-values or sequential tests to avoid false wins

question.en: You have two prompts with similar offline F1, but one is 30% slower. For a support chatbot with strict latency SLOs, what should you do next?

text.en: Ship the slower prompt because it has marginally higher F1
Run an online A/B with latency as a guardrail and deflection rate as the primary KPI
Only check offline toxicity and ignore latency
Average both prompts at runtime to balance trade-offs

explanation.en: Online A/B verifies real impact while enforcing latency guardrails and a meaningful business KPI (deflection rate).

question.en: Your offline eval set contains many near-duplicates from the fine-tuning data of a candidate model. What is the most likely effect?

text.en: Improves generalization by repetition
Data leakage that inflates offline scores and misrepresents true performance
No effect on evaluation quality
Makes online experiments safer

explanation.en: Overlap with fine-tuning data leaks answers and overstates offline performance, reducing external validity.

question.en: Which approach best reduces time to detect a harmful regression during rollout?

text.en: Switch 100% of traffic immediately
Canary rollout with real-time guardrail metrics and sequential testing
Wait 30 days before checking metrics
Rely only on offline evaluation results

explanation.en: Canary plus real-time guardrails and sequential tests enables fast detection and rollback if harm appears.

body.en:
• Use offline evaluation to shortlist safe, promising candidates quickly
• Validate causal impact online with A/B or bandits, enforcing safety and latency guardrails
• Maintain cohort slicing and statistical rigor to avoid false signals and detect regressions

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to version prompts and related artifacts for reproducibility 2) What metadata to log for lineage and audits 3) How to compare versions and roll out changes safely

Treat prompts as first-class, immutable artifacts. Store full template text (system, user, tool instructions), variable names/defaults, and formatting constraints. Version all runtime parameters (temperature, top_p, max_tokens, stop, penalties), the exact model ID and revision, tokenizer, safety filters, and tool or function schemas. Track dependencies: RAG retriever/index versions, knowledge snapshots, guardrail policies, and evaluation datasets. Create an artifact manifest with a content hash and semver tag, and keep lineage links from dataset → prompt → model → release → evaluation results.

Experiment tracking should log inputs (redacted), rendered prompts, parameters, model/version, outputs, tokens, latency, cost, and user feedback. Protect privacy by redacting or hashing identifiers and enforcing access controls. Use CI/CD for prompts: propose changes via review, run offline gates, compare against baselines, then canary or A/B with rollback and change logs. Keep a changelog with semantic diffs of prompts, not just file diffs, to catch meaning-altering edits. Ensure reproducibility by pinning all versions and capturing environment metadata (SDK, provider, region, feature flags).

blocks.title: Deploying and Monitoring LLM Inference Endpoints
blocks.label: Recommended Viewing

body.en:
• Prompt versioning: immutable artifacts with semantic tags and hashes for reliable rollback and reproduction
• Metadata and lineage: log model ID, parameters, tools, RAG index and dataset versions, plus outputs and feedback to trace decisions
• Change management: offline gates → canary/A-B rollout with approvals, monitoring, and clear rollback criteria

question.en: You need to reproduce a user-facing incident from last week. Besides the raw input, what should you retrieve first?

text.en: Only the model family name
Exact prompt template, model revision, temperature, and tool/function definitions used
Cloud region and VM size only
Dashboard color theme

explanation.en: Reproducibility depends on the precise prompt, model/version, and parameters, plus tool schemas that affect behavior.

question.en: What is the best control to prevent accidental prompt edits from reaching production?

text.en: Edit production prompts in place for speed
Tag immutable prompt versions and ship via CI/CD with reviews and approvals
Store prompts only in a wiki page
Rely on team chat confirmations

explanation.en: Versioned artifacts with CI/CD and approvals provide auditability and prevent unreviewed changes from deploying.

question.en: Logging full user messages risks storing PII. What is a recommended approach?

text.en: Disable all logging
Apply configurable redaction and hash or tokenize identifiers before storage
Store everything indefinitely for future analysis
Email logs to the team daily for review

explanation.en: Redaction and tokenization preserve utility while reducing privacy risk; combine with retention limits and access controls.

body.en:
• Treat prompts, parameters, and tool schemas as versioned, immutable artifacts
• Log rich metadata and lineage to enable debugging, audits, and reproducibility
• Use controlled rollout with monitoring and rollback to safely ship prompt and model changes

In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design effective feedback channels and schemas (explicit and implicit) to capture quality, safety, and UX signals 2) How to run a reliable annotation workflow with clear rubrics, rater calibration, and quality control 3) How to transform feedback into training and evaluation datasets that drive iterative model improvement

Quality monitoring depends on systematic feedback loops. Explicit feedback includes user ratings (thumbs up/down), reason codes, and short comments; implicit feedback is derived from behavior such as message edits, abandonment, re-prompts, or downstream task success. A good schema captures context (prompt, system state, retrieved docs), response, user segment, reason codes, and timestamps while respecting privacy (avoid storing raw PII, apply hashing/redaction). Annotation workflows should be driven by a rubric that defines label definitions, edge cases, and decision trees, plus positive/negative examples. Rater calibration uses training rounds, gold/catch trials, and discussion to improve consistency. Inter-annotator agreement (e.g., Cohen’s kappa, Krippendorff’s alpha) quantifies label reliability and guides rubric refinements. Sampling strategies combine stratified sampling across intents/risk tiers with active sampling of outliers (low confidence, drift signals) to maximize learning value. Feedback is triaged into: bug reports (prompt/policy fix), supervision data (fine-tuning/RLHF), and evaluation items (golden sets) to close the loop.

• Feedback types: Explicit (ratings, reason codes) vs. implicit (edits, task success) and how each informs quality signals
• Annotation rubric: Clear criteria, examples, and decision rules to produce consistent, high-signal labels
• Rater quality and IAA: Calibration, gold checks, and agreement metrics (e.g., kappa) to ensure label reliability

question.en: You’re designing a production feedback schema for a chat assistant. Which approach best balances usefulness and reliability for downstream analysis?

text.en: Collect only free-text comments for thumbs-down events
Capture structured reason codes with optional free-text, plus prompt/context and user segment
Store only response IDs to reduce storage costs
Log full raw transcripts including PII for maximum detail

explanation.en: Structured reason codes support reliable aggregation; optional comments add nuance. Capturing context enables root-cause analysis. PII should be minimized/redacted.

question.en: Your team sees low inter-annotator agreement on hallucination labels. What is the most effective next step?

text.en: Increase the number of annotators to average out disagreements
Refine the rubric with concrete examples, run a calibration session, and add gold checks
Reduce label classes to only 'good' and 'bad'
Proceed as-is; training will smooth out label noise

explanation.en: Clarifying criteria, adding examples, and calibrating raters improves consistency; gold/catch trials monitor ongoing reliability.

question.en: With a limited annotation budget, which sampling strategy most improves feedback actionability?

text.en: Uniformly sample recent conversations
Label only satisfied (thumbs-up) cases to learn what's working
Stratify by intent/risk tier and actively sample low-confidence or drifted cases
Annotate every single conversation until the budget runs out

explanation.en: Stratified + active sampling prioritizes coverage of critical segments and uncertain/outlier cases, yielding higher-value insights per label.

body.en:
• Design a privacy-aware feedback schema with structured reason codes and contextual metadata
• Use rubrics, calibration, gold checks, and IAA to ensure label quality
• Route feedback into bug fixes, golden sets, and training data to power continuous improvement
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design feedback channels and run reliable annotation workflows that convert real-world signals into high-quality data.

blocks.title: Monitoring LLM with MLflow | AI Agent Monitoring and Evaluation
blocks.label: Tutorial

body.en: In this lesson you will learn: 1) How to design multi-metric regression gates that compare candidates to a baseline 2) How to handle LLM stochasticity with repeated trials, segment-level analysis, and non-inferiority bounds 3) How to integrate gates into CI/CD with shadow/canary rollout and automatic rollback

Regression gates enforce quality bars before deployment by comparing a candidate model or prompt to a frozen baseline on golden datasets and realistic replay logs. Gates should be multi-metric: task quality (exact match/F1, model-graded utility), safety (toxicity, PII leakage, hallucination), latency, and cost. Because LLMs are stochastic, evaluate with multiple seeds or n-samples per prompt and summarize with means and confidence/credible intervals; require superiority on primary KPIs and non-inferiority (within a guardband) on safety/critical segments. Segment-level gates (e.g., payments, healthcare) prevent masking degradations by global averages. Define pass/fail criteria and allowed deltas up front, and set minimum sample sizes to ensure power. Integrate these checks in CI/CD: automatic eval on PR, fail the build on gate violations, and require approvals for overrides. After passing offline gates, use shadow testing and small canaries with real traffic, monitoring for drift, error budgets, and rollback triggers.

• Golden sets and baselines: Stable reference data and a frozen model/prompt for apples-to-apples comparison
• Guardbands and non-inferiority: Predefined thresholds that prevent regressions on critical metrics and segments
• Shadow/canary rollout: Validate in production with small exposure, strict monitors, and automatic rollback

question.en: A candidate model improves average score but degrades substantially on the 'payments' intent. What should your gate enforce?

text.en: Allow deployment because global average improved
Block unless the 'payments' segment meets its non-inferiority threshold or is fixed
Lower the bar for high-revenue intents to ship faster
Ignore the segment due to smaller sample size

explanation.en: Segment-level gates with guardbands prevent critical regressions from being hidden by overall averages.

question.en: You expect only a ~1 point improvement. How should you account for LLM randomness in gating?

text.en: Run once with a fixed seed to save cost
Evaluate multiple seeds/samples per item and require improvement beyond the confidence interval
Disable sampling and temperature for both models
Rely on manual reviewer judgment only

explanation.en: Multiple trials with interval estimates distinguish real gains from noise; small deltas require statistical confidence.

question.en: Which pre-deployment plan best balances progress with safety when gains are uneven across metrics?

text.en: Use a non-inferiority design with guardbands on safety/critical segments, require superiority on the primary KPI, then shadow/canary with rollback
Pick the metric that looks best and ship to 100% immediately
Waive gates temporarily to accelerate iteration
Gate only on latency and cost to reduce variance

explanation.en: Non-inferiority plus superiority reflects multi-metric risk; progressive rollout validates in real traffic with safety nets.

body.en:
• Use multi-metric, segment-aware gates with predefined thresholds and minimum sample sizes
• Mitigate stochasticity with multi-seed evaluations and confidence intervals; require non-inferiority on critical metrics
• Integrate gates into CI/CD and validate with shadow/canary rollouts and automatic rollback triggers
Congratulations! You have completed this lesson. You can now design and operate robust regression gates that prevent quality and safety regressions before deployment.
